item.title: The Myth That Behavioral Approaches Fail Neurodivergent Kids
item.description:
Autism

The Myth That Behavioral Approaches Fail Neurodivergent Kids

Neurodivergence changes how behavioral tools are used, not whether they work.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Social media pushes the myth that behavioral approaches don't work with neurodivergent kids.
  • Behavioral parent training and PCIT are effective for ADHD, ODD, and kids on the spectrum.
  • Behavioral tools need tailoring for neurodivergent kids, not abandoning them altogether.
Same car, more horsepower.
Source: Author: AI Generated

In online parent support groups for ADHD, autism, and pathological demand avoidance (PDA), one claim comes up again and again: behavioral approaches don't work for neurodivergent kids.

It's voiced most often by influencers and by parents of children and teens on the spectrum with low support needs (Level 1). They're told that rewards and consequences work for neurotypical children, but the neurodivergent brain "doesn't work that way."

This is a factual claim, and it has been tested many times in exactly these children.

What Does "Behavioral" Actually Mean?

Operant learning is a basic learning process, documented in species from fruit flies to humans, in which behavior is shaped by what follows it (Brembs, 2003). There is no evidence that any group of children is exempt from it. A child who gets attention for a tantrum, escapes a hard task by melting down, masks around others is already learning from consequences.

Modern parent training relies mainly on positive attention, specific praise, predictable routines, and calm, brief consequences. Despite what social media often claims, it isn't harsh or punitive.

Some neurodivergent children need reinforcement that is more immediate or intense (Luman et al., 2005), but that changes how it's used, not whether it works.

ADHD: First-Line Treatment

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends parent behavior training as the first-line treatment for preschoolers with ADHD. For children ages 6 to 11, it recommends medication together with parent training (Wolraich et al., 2019). The UK's NICE guideline also names parent training as first-line treatment for children under 5 (NICE, 2018).

Yet parents of children with ADHD who struggle with disruptive behavior and emotion regulation are often steered toward sensory-based occupational therapy or play therapy, even though neither guideline recommends them for ADHD and the research behind them is weak (Zimmer & Desch, 2012).

The evidence for parent behavior training is strong. For preschoolers, a major review rated the evidence as high strength, stronger than for medication (Charach et al., 2013). In school-age children with ADHD whose disruptive behavior persisted despite prior treatment, oppositional symptoms dropped 43% with parent training, versus 24% on a waitlist and 8% with usual care (Nobel et al., 2020). And starting with behavioral treatment produced about one-third fewer classroom rule violations than starting with medication (Pelham et al., 2016).

High-Functioning Autism (Low Support Needs): The Evidence

The RUBI trial randomly assigned 180 autistic children ages 3 to 7 to behavioral parent training or parent education (Bearss et al., 2015). About three-quarters had no intellectual disabilty. With parent training, irritability fell 47.7%, and noncompliance, including avoiding or refusing everyday demands, fell 55.0%, versus 31.8% and 34.2% with parent education. Blinded clinicians rated 68.5% of parent-training children as much or very much improved, versus 39.6%. Neither IQ nor autism severity changed how well the treatment worked (Lecavalier et al., 2017).

A Dutch trial randomly assigned 97 autistic children ages 4 to 13 with disruptive behavior and an average IQ, all referred to ordinary mental health clinics (Dekkers et al., 2026). With face-to-face behavioral parent training, 78.1% showed at least a 25% improvement in noncompliance, versus 42.9% on the waitlist (Breider et al., 2026).

Parent-Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT) coaches parents in real time to use praise and attention, give clear requests, and follow through consistently. In a randomized trial of 55 autistic children ages 4 to 10 without intellectual disability, PCIT reduced disruptive behavior, improved ability to follow directions, and lowered parenting stress compared with a control group. Every child who completed PCIT finished in the non-clinical range on a standard disruptive-behavior measure, regardless of autism severity (Allen et al., 2023).

What About Anxiety and PDA?

The PDA narrative holds that demands trigger anxiety, so behavioral strategies backfire. Yet no controlled trial has shown that low-demand approaches beat behavioral treatment. And anxiety and operant learning are not competing explanations. A demand leads to distress, the distress escalates, and the demand is often withdrawn. The child's relief is momentary, but the avoidance has been strongly reinforced. The anxiety is real, and the avoidance is also being learned.

The treatment that works for anxious autistic children moves toward feared situations, not away from them. In a trial of 167 autistic children with IQs of 70 or above, 92.4% responded to exposure-based CBT adapted for autism, compared with 11.1% in usual care (Wood et al., 2020). Removing every demand may calm things for now while strengthening the avoidance.

"But CPS Works Better": Not Really

Collaborative and Proactive Solutions (CPS) is often mentioned on social media as a more effective alternative to behavioral approaches. CPS has never been tested in a controlled trial with autistic children. In its main trial, 134 youth with oppositional defiant disorder, more than half of whom also had ADHD, were randomly assigned to CPS or behavioral parent training. Both worked equally well: 48.0% of the CPS group and 48.8% of the behavioral group no longer met diagnostic criteria (Ollendick et al., 2016). CPS is a reasonable option, but not a superior one.

Taking Concerns Seriously

Some autistic adults describe painful experiences with outdated, rigid ABA programs that prized compliance over well-being. Those accounts deserve to be heard. But a widely cited survey linking ABA to post-traumatic stress symptoms has been criticized for leading questions, unvalidated measures, and unconfirmed diagnoses (Leaf et al., 2018).

Why Do Parents Believe Behavioral Approaches Don’t Work?

Because, for their especially challenging kids, they haven't. Simple reward charts and basic consequences often fail with highly explosive or demand-avoidant children. Think of these as a small car engine: fine for most kids, underpowered for neurodivergence. In our clinic, we don't replace the engine. We add more horsepower. Most clinicians have not been trained to add that horsepower, and there is a profound shortage of those who have been. The engine isn't the problem. Finding a mechanic who knows how to supercharge it is.

The Bottom Line

If you've tried the reward charts, taken away the tablet, and watched things get worse, it's understandable to conclude these things don’t work. You were handed tools that can work but need to be highly modified.

Your child's brain isn't the exception to how learning works. Bright, anxious, explosive, demand-avoidant kids learn from what follows their behavior every day, like every other child.

How an adult responds to a child’s behavior is one of the most important factors that determines whether that behavior will get worse, stay the same, or improve over time. That is the essence of parent-driven behavioral interventions.

So don't abandon structure, praise, and consequences. Find a competent therapist well-trained in behavioral interventions, and ask how they'll adapt them for your child. Your child deserves help that has actually been tested. So do you.

item.title: 7 Signs Your Spouse Is Checking Out of Your Marriage
item.description:
Marriage

7 Signs Your Spouse Is Checking Out of Your Marriage

How a spouse withdraws emotionally before ever saying they want to leave.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Paying attention to subtle changes in communication can reveal a lot.
  • Small changes in affection and daily habits can point to deeper issues.
  • One sign alone may mean little, but new patterns demand attention.
Spouse checked out of marriage.
Source: engin akyurt/Unsplash

Even if it appears your spouse just up and left without a thought, chances are there were signs they were checking out long before. Signs you may not have noticed or that you subconsciously ignored.

No matter how you got here, the proverb “Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me” can inspire you to regain control of your life. Whether you and your spouse have decided to reconcile or you want to learn from the past and be more present with someone new, identifying behaviors that suggest your spouse may be checking out of your marriage can keep you from being blindsided.

They Communicate Less

Instead of saying, “Let’s talk,” people who are checking out of a marriage tend to do the opposite: They say nothing. But not necessarily regarding the practical matters that keep the home running, like whose turn it is to empty the dishwasher or whether they’ll be home for dinner. The silence is subtler, and evident in what they don't say.

For example, the withdrawing spouse may no longer tell you about their day or ask you to come to bed. They may stop bringing up what’s been bothering them, like an issue at work, or no longer ask if you noticed they got their hair trimmed or bought a new lamp for the living room. Most evidently, they stop fighting for what they once did in the marriage. If you’re not paying attention, you could easily miss these signs or dismiss them, attributing them to another cause.

Their Body Language Changes

Beyond the words, and even when the language still feels familiar, a spouse with one foot out the door often exhibits changes in their body language. They may no longer move in for the hug, pick up your hand to hold it, initiate sex, or, if you initiate it, want to engage. They may flinch if you touch them, turn their back on you in bed, or cross their arms when you talk to them.

Body language is reflexive and can’t hide what words can. If you’re attuned to these changes, you may realize something is, or has been, going on beneath the surface.

They’re Not As Considerate at Home

When a spouse cares about you, they demonstrate it. They bring you a cup of coffee, put out a clean bath towel if you forgot, and heat up your dinner when you’re on the way home.

If these behaviors were present before and then slowly disappear, it can signal that your spouse is less invested in you. Again, this can happen temporarily if someone is overwhelmed or busy. However, when it becomes the new status quo, it’s time to question why.

They Change Their Appearance

Many people who discover their spouse is having an affair say their spouse made changes in their physical appearance. This can be buying new clothes, changing their hairstyle, or wearing makeup when they didn’t before.

Of course, these behaviors don’t have to indicate an affair or even a loss of interest in the marriage. Instead, they can reveal something as simple as exercising self-care where they hadn’t before. But they could mean more, and if you see not just one but several of these outward changes, you may want to look for possible reasons, including that your spouse no longer wants to be with you.

They Stop Explaining (or Explain More)

When someone in a healthy marriage leaves for an errand or activity, they typically say goodbye and let the other person know where they’re going: “Going to the grocery store, do you need anything?” or “I’ll be a few minutes late tonight because I need to fill up the car.”

When these small explanations for someone’s whereabouts stop, along with their willingness to serve you or keep you from worrying, it’s time to take notice. Naturally, people can forget from time to time, so you’re looking for consistency.

On the flip side, when someone explains too much about where they were or where they’re going, it can also be that they’re hiding something. Though it doesn’t have to mean they’re cheating, even leaving you out of an activity you might normally be a part of can indicate they no longer care about whether you’re there or your feelings.

They Become More Independent

Becoming more independent in a marriage can similarly indicate that a spouse is preparing to leave. One of the most obvious signs is if your spouse isolates their money from yours, or does so more than usual. Or they save for or make large purchases, such as a new home, car, or boat, and don’t include you in the decision-making.

A spouse who hasn’t worked outside the home in years suddenly wanting to go back to school to increase their marketability, or picking up their career where they left off, can likewise signal that they want more independence, and that they want it to get away from you. Of course, there can be many reasons why a person wants more independence. That being said, without the communication to accompany the change, it can and should leave you wondering.

They Hint That They’re Not Happy

Perhaps the most obvious sign your spouse is checking out is that they tell you. They may not be blunt about it (“I’m not happy here anymore.”) but, instead, say something less forthcoming, even phrasing it as a question to gauge your feelings: “I’m kind of feeling blah these days and may need to make some changes in my life,” or "How do you think things are going between us lately?”

Not asking a follow-up question, or answering “Fine” to the latter and ending the conversation, can leave your spouse wanting to communicate but unsure how to speak to you. And no alternative but to “surprise” you by leaving when, in reality, you didn’t have to be surprised and could’ve worked on your issues together.

item.title: Self-Validation vs. Validation From Others
item.description:
Identity

Self-Validation vs. Validation From Others

When validation types don't coincide, psychological distress is inevitable.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Conscious judgments about the self are often the building blocks of personal identity.
  • Underlying most behavior are tacit assumptions and autopilot judgments about the self.
  • Misalignment of conscious and autopilot judgments about the self creates a need for validation from others.

Self-validation: the feeling of having recognized, confirmed, or established one's own worthiness or legitimacy. –Webster’s Dictionary

Articles I’ve read about self-validation present it as a series of conscious judgments about the self. Conscious judgments about the self are often the building blocks of personal identity. When conscious self-validation is a building block of identity, the identity it builds is likely to be insecure and difficult to maintain, requiring a certain amount of adrenaline to assert in public. Here's why.

The underlying factors in most behavior are tacit assumptions about the self and the autopilot judgments that derive from them. Conscious judgments are easy to discern. Discovering our tacit assumptions and autopilot judgments takes effort, if not psychotherapy.

Without attention to tacit assumptions, the risks of conscious self-validation are self-deception and hypocrisy, if not outright phoniness. Think of SNL character Stuart Smalley—a lovable mass of insecurity—reciting in the mirror: “I'm good enough, I'm smart enough, and doggone it, people like me!”

Of course, tacit self-validation has its own risks. Even when there is little delusion involved, it has a veneer of self-satisfaction, which can inhibit emotional growth and flexibility.

Validation From Others

Most people like validation from others, although we tend to want it—demand it—more than we give it. Demanding respect is often in itself disrespectful.

The desire for validation is based on how we want others to perceive us. It always has some degree of impression management. As the desire for validation expands into a perceived need for it, impression management expands commensurately. When that happens, validation from others may feel phony, undeserved, or never quite enough.

Even when emotional validation doesn’t seem phony or undeserved, the good feeling we get from it lasts about as long as the mellow feeling provided by an alcoholic drink.

Nothing makes us more susceptible to manipulation and exploitation than a perceived need for validation. Bad actors seem able to detect those who feel in need of validation. Self-validation is the most effective protection from manipulation, exploitation, and abuse.

The Validation Paradox of Politics

We tend to vote for politicians who validate our feelings and opinions, more often than we vote for those who stand for what’s best for the country. This is a major reason why so many voters experience buyer’s remorse when their candidates win and move away from validation toward pragmatic governance.

Politicians certainly need validation from voters. But not from any one voter or, in our polarized times, any one group of voters. When I was young, politicians validated the consensus. Now they play one group against the other. It’s not enough to validate one group, they must invalidate, if not demonize the other.

Building Self-Validation

The most important step in building genuine self-validation is to test our tacit assumptions. The surest way to discover our tacit assumptions is to infer them from what we resent about others

"Everything that irritates us about others can lead to an understanding of ourselves.” –Carl Jung

For example, if I resent someone whom I think doesn't recognize facts, the possible tacit assumptions are:

  • Uninformed people are inferior.
  • My interpretations of facts (and supporting evidence) are superior to those who disagree with me.
  • Disagreement is disrespect.

The next step is to decide whether I really believe these assumptions and whether they reflect my deeper values. If so, I validate them. If not, I endeavor to change them by practicing behaviors that reflect my deeper values.

item.title: What Does Penetration Actually 'Feel' Like?
item.description:
Sex

What Does Penetration Actually 'Feel' Like?

Why assuming your partner feels what you feel gets in the way of better sex.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Many lovers assume sexual intercourse feels the same for both partners.
  • The vagina, clitoris, and penis are anatomically wired to detect different sensations.
  • In a new study, men and women were found to hold markedly different beliefs about sensations in intercourse.

What does a vagina or penis actually ‘feel’ (during penetration)? It's a surprisingly difficult question to answer. We know quite a lot about genital anatomy, but we know much less about how people actually experience the physical sensations of intercourse. We talk about orgasm, sexual desire, and satisfaction. Much less often do we ask about the sensation itself.

I didn't expect that to become such an important question in my career. And I certainly didn't expect one colleague to tell me that answering it changed his sex life.

The Conversation That Stayed With Me

A few years ago, I shared the results of one of my studies with a colleague. We talked about it for a few minutes and then moved on. Then, a few weeks ago, he stopped me for a hallway conversation. "You probably don't remember telling me about that study," he said, "but it completely challenged how I thought about sex."

That surprised me. He wasn't someone who lacked knowledge about sexuality. Although he is not a sex therapist, he's spent his career as a counsellor, deeply committed to helping people build healthy relationships. He understood the importance of the clitoris and had always cared about his partners' pleasure. By most people's standards, he was already a thoughtful lover.

Yet he admitted that he had been unknowingly carrying a problematic assumption for his entire adult life. He assumed his partner experienced intercourse in her vagina much the same way he experienced it in his penis. It was a belief he had never questioned. Why would he? None of us know what someone else is experiencing. Our partner's experience can only ever be imagined—unless we ask.

As a sex therapist myself, I began to suspect that this assumption was not all that rare. Clients in my practice often described intercourse (penis-vagina) as though it should naturally feel intensely stimulating for everyone involved. That made me wonder how widespread this assumption really was.

The Question

Ironically, this question became clearer while I was working on a completely different research project. I was analyzing pornography. Like most people, I already knew pornography exaggerates reality. What caught my attention was something more subtle. The women in many scenes appeared to experience extraordinarily intense sensations from intercourse alone—as though vaginal stimulation produced sensations every bit as intense as the man experienced from the penis.

While popular culture often implies heterosexual intercourse should feel the same for both lovers, anatomy suggests a more complicated story. The vagina and the penis are remarkable organs, but they are not built the same way. Their sensory anatomy differs, which raises an obvious question: Does sexual intercourse actually produce the same intensity of pleasurable sensation for both partners?

Surprisingly, I couldn't find a study that answered that question directly. So we decided to ask it ourselves. In a larger study I was conducting on orgasm (presented at SSTAR, 2026), we included a question that asked participants to rate the intensity of the pleasurable sensations they experienced in their penis or vagina during their most recent experience of penile-vaginal intercourse. Study details here. We asked specifically about vaginal sensation on its own, apart from the clitoris, since the clitoris may or may not be stimulated during intercourse. We weren't asking who enjoyed intercourse more, who orgasmed, or who had better sex. We were asking about the intensity of the sensation itself.

Sexual intercourse can involve intense pleasurable sensations without leading to orgasm. It can also involve relatively subtle sensations while still feeling deeply intimate, emotionally meaningful, or sexually satisfying. In other words, pleasurable intensity is one piece of the larger puzzle of sexual intercourse—not the whole picture.

What We Discovered

The results were striking. Women were more likely than men to describe the intensity of pleasurable sensations in their vagina as low or moderate in intensity. Men, on the other hand, were more likely to report highly intense pleasurable sensations in their penis during intercourse.

This finding doesn't tell us who enjoys sex more. Nor does it tell us who has better sex. It tells us something much more specific: the level of intensity of (pleasurable) sensations reported during intercourse is not the same for everyone.

That finding is consistent with what we know about anatomy. The penis and vagina are different organs with different sensory structures, so it shouldn't surprise us that they can produce different sensory experiences. The vagina, clitoris, and penis are anatomically wired to detect different sensations, more here.

This lines up with other research where women have reported the vagina to be less sexually sensitive than the external genitalia, allowing the strongest, easiest orgasms to come from the area on and above the clitoris (Schober et al., 2004). And most women require (or are helped) by clitoral stimulation to orgasm during intercourse (Herbenick et al., 2018).

What People Thought Their Partners Felt

The next question interested me even more. After asking people about their own experiences, participants were asked what they believed was true for the other person. Which organ do you think experiences stronger pleasurable sensations during intercourse—the penis or the vagina?

What men and women believed the other's genitals 'feel' during intercourse.
Source: Intensity of Penis-Vagina Sensations During Heterosexual Intercourse, Petra Zebroff

The difference was striking. Two-thirds of women believed the penis feels more during intercourse. Men were far less sure. Among nearly 6,000 men and women surveyed, 59.2% of men thought the vagina feels at least as strong as the penis, if not stronger.

What struck me wasn't whether either group was "right." It was that many of us appear to begin our sexual relationships with very different assumptions about what intercourse feels like for the other person.

Why I Think This Matters

Our assumptions aren't necessarily the problem. We all make them. The problem is that assumptions replace curiosity. When we believe we already know what our partner experiences, we stop asking. And when we stop asking, we give up one of the best chances we have to actually know each other.

One of the most meaningful questions you can ask your partner is not, "Did you orgasm?" It is, "What did that actually feel like for you?" There is no ‘right’ answer. There's only their answer. Some people experience intercourse as intensely stimulating. Others experience it as emotionally powerful but physically more subtle. Many find that the most pleasurable parts of sex involve much more than intercourse alone. None of those experiences is wrong. They are simply different. And if we never talk about them, our partners are left to fill in the blanks with their own assumptions.

Perhaps that's what my colleague discovered. He realized that his partner might not experience intercourse in anything like the way he did. It changed how he listened. He assumed less. Became more curious. And, in the end, more connected.

Maybe that's the real lesson from this research. The best sex doesn't come from believing we already understand each other's bodies. It begins the moment we realize we don't.

I think that's a pretty good place to start.

One way to start the conversation about what sex feels like is by taking the questionnaire yourself, then send your partner the link to take their own version. You'll each get a private report—and a way to compare notes, together, when you're ready. Take the penetration questionnaire here.

item.title: So Far Gone: Chaos With a Messy, But Real, Resolution
item.description:
Relationships

So Far Gone: Chaos With a Messy, But Real, Resolution

Book Review: Rhys Kinnick faces a crisis of sanity and takes us along

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • In So Far Gone, author Jess Walter writes with wit, energy, and relatable characters.
  • Rhys Kinnick is a multidimensional creature you have to love, while you’re questioning his good sense.
  • His daughter Bethany thinks her dad is disappointed in her, and Rhys is sure he’s the disappointment.
  • “I felt like the world was drifting in one direction and I was going the other way,” Rhys says.

Protagonist Rhys Kinnick is like many contemporary journalists—unemployed, cynical, and hyper-aware of the chaos of the world. Once a respected environmental investigative reporter, he’s one of the many victims of mass layoffs throughout the media and, in his 50s, has no remotely similar prospects. Add to this a strained relationship with his beloved daughter Bethany, a son-in law who has become a Christian nationalist, a failed romantic entanglement, and the fallout from the 2016 election, and Rhys faces a crisis of sanity. “I felt like the world was drifting in one direction and I was going the other way,” he says.

The final straw is a disastrous Thanksgiving dinner conversation with his son-in-law Shane, in which both men are absolutely right, and Rhys unravels. He drives to his family’s 40-acre sheep farm outside of Spokane, on which sheep likely have never set a hoof, throws his cell phone (“a $600 Pop-Tart of modern science”) out the window, and becomes as close to a hermit as he can manage. For seven years, he lives off the grid, filling his small cabin with hundreds of books and thousands of pages of his own writing. Outside, he begins destroying outbuildings in an attempt to gradually eliminate all signs of his existence.

Rhys is not a man for subtlety.

When his two delightful grandchildren show up at his front porch, he doesn’t recognize them at first. Leah, 13, and Asher, 6, are delivered to him by one of their neighbors after Bethany has disappeared. Asher, with his grandfather’s sense of drama, suggests perhaps his father has killed his mother. Nobody believes him, nor should they. Meanwhile, Shane is off being masculine and godly in the woods at the Church of the Blessed Fire.

All this aside, Asher needs to get to a chess tournament that night because he says he is a prodigy. This is also not true. But the kid loves chess, and Rhys, with a renewed sense of grandfatherly connection, rises to the occasion.

But first, he needs a shower and a haircut because his cabin has only the most basic indoor plumbing. (He will need at least a second shower, plus new clothes, to be minimally fit for civilization.) His friend Joanie will do the cut, but only after her common-law husband Brian scuffles with Rhys in the driveway over a slight miscommunication over Rhys’s affection for Joanie. Such is Rhys’s life.

Once somewhat clean and coiffed, he and Leah and Asher head to the Episcopal church for the tournament. But Bethany got the night wrong and there’s no tournament, only Army of our Lord (AOL) thugs waiting for them. Rhys ends up with a fractured zygomatic arch from the butt of a gun. The kids get taken to the Rampart, the cult’s compound and, from there, the caper is on. Rhys eventually rescues the kids and Bethany—or, more accurately, they rescue one another.

The characters in this book are beautifully drawn. Rhys is a multidimensional creature you have to love, while you’re questioning his good sense. Asher lives in his imagination, where he is a soldier leaping a mighty river, while awaiting his chess destiny. He’s disarmingly curious and thrilled when he meets real-life “Indians” in Brian and Joanie. Leah has her grandfather’s affinity for words—she describes his dirty beige shirt as being the color or “twice-plowed snow” and his hair like “hash browns and country gravy.” Bethany thinks her dad is disappointed in her, and Rhys is sure he’s the disappointment. Shane is a good father and husband, but fearful for the safety of his family and naïve enough to be susceptible to the lure of a cult.

Rhys faces the aftermath of his own journalistic prowess when the violent man he dubbed the Dominion Eagle Killer in multiple investigative reports ends up a member of AOL, and is especially embittered toward Rhys, who he feels was instrumental in sending him to prison.

Author Jess Walter writes with wit and energy that propels the story forward with an ironic momentum. And his paragraphs can pack a punch:

As a journalist. As an American, as a rationalist, Kinnick had come to terms with the fact that 20 percent of his countrymen were greedy assholes. But then in 2016, the greedy assholes joined with the idiot assholes and the paranoid assholes in what turned out to be an unbeatable constituency. Kinnick realizing that the asshole ceiling was much higher than he’d thought, perhaps half the country. Whatever the number, it was more than he could bear. Especially when they were in his own family.

Walter finds a messy resolution to this chaos, with an explicitly violent passage at the end. Was the violence necessary? It was jarring, and the reality is, we have discovered that some people are so far gone we cannot reason with them.

But who is so far gone here? Rhys? Shane? The Dominion Eagle Killer? The country? Walter seems to say it’s all the above.

Celia, Rhys’s former wife, dies before the novel begins, but remains a voice of familial love and commitment throughout the book. It’s partially through her spirit that Bethany finally welcomes Rhys back home, each a little less disappointed in the other. As for the rest of the world? Well, that’s still a bit of a mess

item.title: From Sinatra to Swift: The Long Arc of Groove and Entrainment
item.description:
Binaural Beats

From Sinatra to Swift: The Long Arc of Groove and Entrainment

Machines may perfect the science of sway but won't replace the soul behind the beat.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Syncing biological rhythms with others actively increases prosocial behavior and reduces isolation.
  • The brain releases dopamine when predicting a beat, driving a natural psychological urge to move.
  • Interpersonal synchrony acts as the unseen connective tissue for highly collaborative organizations.
Art Is That Whisper in Your Ear.
Source: Sara Sherman, used with permission

We were listening to a classic Sinatra record the other day—"Fly Me to the Moon"—and caught our feet tapping long before we even realized the music had started. Later that same week, we watched a video of a stadium literally shaking to Taylor Swift’s "Cruel Summer," with 70,000 people moving together like a single, synchronized organism.

The sonic landscapes of 1956 and 2026 couldn't be more different. But underneath all the noise, the cognitive architecture at work remains exactly the same. We are witnessing a profound, deeply human kind of resonance: the mind’s natural pull toward groove and entrainment.

The Science of the Sway

In cognitive psychology, entrainment is simply what happens when our internal rhythms sync up with the room. This phenomenon describes our internal metronomes—our heart rates, our brainwaves, our motor neurons—locking onto an external beat, or more importantly, onto each other.

Groove provides the psychological push. The irresistible sensation compelling us to move is deeply rooted in the brain's basal ganglia and reward pathways. When a rhythm hits just right, our brains successfully predict the next beat, triggering a release of dopamine. We don’t just passively hear the music; our neurology literally tunes to the frequency, and we experience the sound physically. Crucially, entrainment goes beyond tapping a foot to act as a profound evolutionary tool for social cohesion. When our biology syncs with those around us, prosocial behavior increases and feelings of isolation decrease.

The Architecture of Synchrony

We can easily spot this collective tuning in different forms. Think of the intimate, shared pocket of a mid-century jazz ensemble or the vast scale of a classical symphony. Without a rigid click-track to guide them, a live orchestra relies entirely on interpersonal synchrony to navigate complex pieces. Consider the hypnotic, relentless build of Ravel's Boléro, which slowly pulls the entire room into its pulse, or the intricate, conversational timing required to perform a Mozart string quartet. The musicians stay in the pocket by relying on breathing, eye contact, and micro-movements.

Fast forward to a modern pop stadium, and you see mass hyper-entrainment. The medium shifts from a smoky club or concert hall to a flashing arena, but the psychological goal is identical: creating a shared emotional and physical frequency.

Cultivating the Resonant Mind

So, how do we take this concept of "collective tuning" off the stage and into our daily lives? Interpersonal entrainment is the unseen connective tissue of strong communities and healthy organizations. Think about the best teams you’ve been a part of. They rarely operate through rigid, traditional management; they operate like a jazz ensemble. Everyone is listening, adjusting, and finding the groove together.

Cultivating a "resonant mind" means actively tuning in to the pacing, energy, and emotional rhythms of the people around us. This cultivation requires acute metacognition—an awareness of not just what you are contributing, but how your personal rhythm affects the whole. A true system architect doesn't just dictate the tempo; they listen for the resonance. When a group finds a shared rhythm, collaboration feels less like a forced task and more like a natural, synchronized movement.

Resonance in Practice: Classrooms, Boardrooms, and Elevators

If entrainment acts as a neurological tool for cohesion, we can intentionally design spaces that foster such connection:

  • The Classroom and Whole-School Setting: Imagine a school that uses a specific, rhythmic 60-BPM track during passing periods. This soundtrack isn't just about managing the clock. The rhythm actively down-regulates the students' nervous systems, anchoring their executive function and preparing their cognitive architecture for the next lesson before they even sit down.
  • The Boardroom: Instead of jumping cold into a high-stakes strategy session, what if team meetings began with a brief, shared audio cue or a collective moment of focused breathing? Aligning the room's collective rhythm increases prosocial behavior and sets the stage for genuine collaboration rather than top-down management.
  • The Bio-Responsive Elevator (A Fun Concept): Let's rethink elevator music. Traditionally, Muzak is bland background noise. But imagine an algorithmic, bio-responsive elevator that reads the collective heart rate of stressed corporate passengers. The system generates a track on the fly, starting at a frantic 90 BPM and gently entraining the riders down to a calm 70 BPM by the time the doors open in the lobby.

The Enduring Beat: AI and the Future of Music

As we look to the future, music creation will become increasingly entangled with artificial intelligence. We are already seeing algorithms generate hyper-personalized tracks engineered specifically to entrain our brainwaves for deep focus or restorative sleep. While machines may soon perfect the clinical science of the sway, they cannot replace the human soul behind the beat.

Ultimately, our brains are the true intelligence, not the artificial models. Regardless of what the future may bring, we remain the conductors of our own lives—always searching for shared human resonance, and always finding the rhythm together.
